children.text: A Portfolio Manager cannot manage nineteen components directly. Below the portfolio sits the program level, and in the five-pillar framework the programs are the pillars themselves. Each pillar needs a program manager who manages its components as a coherent whole and answers to the Portfolio Manager for them.

This lesson describes the five pillar program manager roles in Chapter 15, the credentials that fit them, and the three-tier governance structure PMI defines for a portfolio. It closes with what changes when the same structure is built inside a hospital rather than a state agency.

Structure is the part of portfolio management that organizations most often skip, because it feels like overhead. The book's argument is that it is the opposite: without it, the coordination work still has to happen, but it happens informally, inconsistently and invisibly.
Each Pillar Is a Program

In PMI's terms, a program is a group of related projects managed together for benefits no single project could deliver. Chapter 15 treats each pillar as exactly that. The Technology pillar's components, the analytics platform, the health information exchange, the Care Integration Network and the AI-governance framework, only produce a usable data substrate together. The Economics pillar's components only change hospital incentives together.

So each pillar needs a designated accountability point with the skills and authority to manage its components as one program. The book is careful that these roles are not exclusive to the state agency. For hospital-owned components, the program manager may sit in a hospital's project office; for state-administered components, in AHS. What matters is that every pillar has one.

The pillar program manager's distinctive job is managing interdependencies inside the pillar and reporting the pillar's readiness upward, because the pillar's readiness is what opens or closes the gate for the pillars downstream of it.
A pillar program manager owns two things a project manager does not: the dependencies between the pillar's own components, and the pillar's readiness as an input to every pillar downstream.
Five Roles, One Framework

Figure 15.4 of the book sets out the five roles. Each pairs a project-management credential with domain experience, names the key deliverables the role is accountable for, and specifies a dual reporting line: to the Portfolio Manager for the portfolio, and to the domain leader who owns the pillar's subject matter.

The dual reporting is deliberate. The Payment Reform Program Manager answers both to the Portfolio Manager and to the Green Mountain Care Board's executive director, because the board owns hospital budgets and pricing. The Clinical Transformation Program Manager answers to the Portfolio Manager and to the Blueprint director and Medicaid medical director, because clinical programs run through them. Dual reporting keeps the program manager connected to both the portfolio's logic and the domain's expertise.

Notice that the deliverables are dated and specific: analytics vendor operational by January 2027, reference-based-pricing rates in effect for FY2028, 100% patient-centered medical home coverage by FY2028, the portfolio office operational by the second quarter of 2027. A program manager is accountable for outcomes with dates, not for activity.

children.text: The Credentials: PMP and PMI-ACP

The book recommends PMI's Project Management Professional (PMP) credential for every pillar role, with PMI's Agile Certified Practitioner (PMI-ACP) credential added where a pillar's work is adaptive. The PMP is the general credential for leading projects. PMI's current eligibility rules offer three paths: a secondary diploma with 60 months of project-management experience; a bachelor's degree with 36 months; or a degree from a GAC-accredited program with 24 months. The first two also require 35 hours of project-management education, which a CAPM certification can satisfy, and experience counts within the past eight years.

The PMI-ACP covers agile methods. PMI requires 21 contact hours of formal training in agile practices together with agile project experience; published summaries of the exact experience rules differ, so candidates should check PMI's current handbook. Lesson 8 of this course explains why the book pairs PMI-ACP with the Technology and Policy roles in particular: the AI-governance framework, the Care Integration Network build-out and parts of rulemaking evolve faster than a fixed plan can anticipate.

As with the PfMP, the credential signals method rather than guaranteeing results. The book's pairing of each credential with specific domain experience, health policy, informatics, finance, clinical practice or hospital turnaround, reflects that pillar program managers have to understand the substance of their components well enough to judge when one is truly ready.

children.text: Three Governance Tiers

PMI defines three tiers of portfolio governance. The Portfolio Governance Body provides strategic oversight: it sets direction, approves the portfolio's composition and makes decisions above the Portfolio Manager's authority. For Vermont, the book identifies this body as the AHS Secretary together with the HCAC and the Green Mountain Care Board. The Portfolio Management Office provides operational coordination; in Vermont that is currently the under-resourced AHS Health Reform Office. The component level is the individual programs and projects.

The first of the five objections answered in Chapter 15 turns on this distinction. Asked whether the HCAC and monthly reports already provide portfolio management, the book replies that the HCAC is a governance body, not a portfolio office. It provides oversight, not an integrated master schedule, resource-conflict resolution, a maintained risk register or earned-value tracking. The HCAC is the governance tier; it needs a Portfolio Manager and an office to give it the data to govern.

The book lists the gaps that establishing the portfolio office must fill: a dedicated Portfolio Manager with the PfMP credential, two PMO analysts, portfolio-management software, standardized reporting, the five pillar program managers, and formal project leads for all nineteen components.

children.text: The Same Structure Inside a Hospital

A hospital or health system running its own transformation faces the same structural problem at smaller scale. Its governance body is the board or a board committee. Its portfolio office is the transformation or strategy office. Its programs may map to the five pillars, or to service lines with the pillars as a cross-check. What carries over is the principle: each level exists, is staffed, and knows which decisions belong to it.

The book's advice to hospital project-office leaders is to treat Figure 15.3 as a template. Build the inventory, assign each component a pillar, an owner, a type and a stage gate, and then assign each pillar an accountable program lead. Small organizations can combine roles, one person leading two pillars, but should not leave a pillar without a named lead.

Hospitals also sit inside the state's portfolio. Several of Vermont's components are hospital-owned, and the fourteen hospital transformation plans are a single Operations program at state level. A hospital whose own portfolio office maps cleanly onto the state's pillars makes coordination with the state far easier, because both sides then speak about the same components in the same terms.
Combining roles is acceptable in a small organization. Leaving a pillar with no named program lead is not; that pillar's dependencies will go unmanaged.

points: In the five-pillar framework each pillar is a program: its components only deliver their benefit together.
Every pillar needs a designated program manager, who may sit in the state agency or in a hospital project office depending on who owns the components.
The five roles in Figure 15.4 pair a PMP with domain experience, carry dated deliverables and report both to the Portfolio Manager and to a domain leader.
PMP eligibility requires 60, 36 or 24 months of project experience depending on education; PMI-ACP requires 21 hours of agile training plus agile experience.
PMI's three governance tiers are the governance body, the portfolio office and the component level; Vermont's governance body is the AHS Secretary with the HCAC and GMCB.
The HCAC is a governance body, not a portfolio office; it needs a Portfolio Manager and an office to supply the data it governs with.
Hospitals can mirror the same structure at smaller scale, combining roles if needed but never leaving a pillar without a named lead.

body.explanation: PMI separates the governance tier, which provides oversight and makes strategic decisions, from the portfolio office, which runs the operational machinery. The book's answer is that the HCAC is the right governance body but needs a Portfolio Manager and an office to give it the data it needs to govern; it does not replace either.
